page: Microsoft Azure B2ms is a burstable virtual machine belonging to the BS family, running on the Microsoft Hyper-V hypervisor. It features an Intel Xeon 8272CL processor with an x86_64 architecture, operating at a clock speed of 2.6 GHz. The server is configured with 2 vCPUs, 2 physical cores, and 1.0 thread per core, providing a burstable CPU allocation model. It includes 8.0 GB of system memory, yielding 4.0 GB of RAM per core. The processor features a 35 MB L3 cache, 1.0 MB L2 cache, and 32 KB L1d cache, with support for AVX, AVX512F, AES, BMI2, ADX, and FMA instruction sets. Local storage consists of 16 GB, and the instance is Premium Storage capable. No GPUs are included.

Benchmark results indicate that the B2ms instance operates primarily in the lower performance tiers. In CPU-bound tests, the server achieved a stress-ng single-core score of 1245.98 and a multi-core score of 2456.99, both falling into the bottom 25% category. Geekbench scores further reflect this limitation, with a single-core score of 1067.0 and a multi-core score of 1976.0, which is in the bottom 10%. Cryptographic and physics simulations also showed lower-tier performance, with a Passmark CPU encryption score of 914.67 and a physics score of 389.34. Memory bandwidth tests recorded 178.56 GB/sec for cached small blocks and 23.73 GB/sec for uncached large blocks, placing memory performance in the bottom 25%.

Due to its burstable CPU allocation and lower overall benchmark scores, the B2ms is best suited for low-intensity workloads that experience periodic spikes in activity. It is appropriate for small-scale database operations, basic web serving, and lightweight development environments. In testing, static web serving throughput reached 2.75 GB/sec, and Redis SET operations achieved 3.07 million operations per second. While LLM text generation for a small 135M model reached an average speed of 94.9 tokens per second, prompt processing was limited to 308.45 tokens per second. The instance offers a cost-efficient entry point for non-continuous workloads but presents significant performance tradeoffs for sustained compute-heavy tasks.
